newsitem.title: USA: Albright offers new post-Saddam ties to Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Albright offers new post-Saddam ties to Iraq.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday affirmed U.S. intentions to back a political opposition in Iraq and laid out for the first time an explicit U.S. commitment to improve ties with a new government in Baghdad if one comes to power.

The State Department denied she was urging an overthrow of Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein, who has been the target of relentless U.S. opposition since Washington in 1991 led an international coalition to repel Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.

But Albright's speech to Georgetown University represents "the first time that the administration has explicitly addressed the issue of how we might deal with a successor regime," a U.S. official said on condition of anonymity.

The official said the speech was the culmination of a review of U.S. policy toward Iraq begun several months ago when Saddam's military forces entered northern Iraq after fighting broke out between rival Kurdish forces there.
The Iraqi incursion disrupted U.S. operations in the region, including a Central Intelligence Agency-funded operation to destabilize the Iraqi government.
Albright, at the university where she taught international relations, reasserted a long-standing hard-line U.S. policy, including indefinite backing for tough U.N. sanctions on Iraq.

And she warned that a recently approved U.N. program allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months for food and medicine "will cease" if Baghdad did not live up to its promises to adhere to very strict conditions.
But she also made clear Iraq could redeem itself with a change to more peaceful leadership.

"Clearly, a change in Iraq's government could lead to a change in U.S. policy. Should that occur, we would stand ready, in coordination with our allies and friends, to enter rapidly into a dialogue with the successor regime," she said.
The dialogue would have two goals. First, to verify that the new Iraq would be "independent, unified and free from undue external influence, for example, from Iran," she said.
Second, the United States would require "improvements in behavior," such as compliance with U.N. resolutions relating to the Gulf War and respect for human rights, she said.

"If our concerns were addressed satisfactorily, Iraq would no longer threaten regional security. Its isolation would end (and) the international community ... would look for ways to ease Iraq's re-integration," she said.
A "whole range of economic and security matters would be open for discussion in a climate of cooperation and mutual respect," she said without elaborating.
U.S. officials have often met Iraqi opposition groups but have had little success in encourging cooperation among them.

Albright vowed Washington "will continue to support the establishment of a coherent and united Iraqi opposition which represents the country's ethnic and confessional diversity." The roadmap toward improved ties she laid out aimed to give hope that Washington would help once Saddam was gone.
Despite setting out this roadmap, Albright, who led the charge against Iraq for four years as U.N. ambassador, showed little confidence of early change in Baghdad.

"If past is prologue, under the current government, an Iraq released from sanctions and scrutiny would pick up where it left off half a dozen years ago," when Iraq invaded Kuwait and built a nuclear and chemical arms arsenal, she said.
"For these reasons, our policy will not change, she said.

"To those who ask how long our determination will last, how long we will oppose Iraqi intransigence, how long we will insist that the international community's standards are met, our answer is -- as long as it takes," she said.

"The evidence is overwhelming that Saddam Hussein's intentions will never be peaceful," she said, renewing charges Iraq has yet to comply with U.N. demands, like proving weapons of mass destruction have been destroyed.
Until there is a positive leadership change in Iraq, Washington will retain the military capability in the region to ensure Iraq does not again attack its neighbors, she vowed.
